articles.title: Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent
articles.summary: Regents Park, London This year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesque.
body: Naked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park.

And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art.

articles.title: This dripless oil can is the prettiest thing in my kitchen – and surprisingly practical
articles.summary: Holcomb Studios’ tabletop oil can is the upgrade your snack time – and kitchen – needs. Five reasons you need a fish spatula, even if you hate fish. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: I f an unfortunate incident befell and I was somehow forced to repopulate my kitchenware, I’d be OK with all of it being gone with the exception of one item – the shiny little oil can I use almost every single day. In a life that is often more complicated than it needs to be, simple pleasures can’t be underrated, and this one is among the nicest.

If the Wizard of Oz’s Tin Man went to Design Within Reach for an upgrade, this oil can would be the result – a tall and sexy stainless steel vessel with a long, skinny spout and a delicate handle, pretty enough to keep out on the dining table. It comes from Holcomb Studio, a delightful new tableware brand out of the Pacific north-west, run by a father and daughter duo. The pair make elegant, beautiful and reasonably priced kitchen goods and I do own a fair amount of their stuff, but nothing really compares to the oil can.

articles.title: One week a year I escape my ‘real’ life as broke standup comic – and travel back to medieval times | Scout Boxall
articles.summary: Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat.
body: Every Friday night on a community sports field in Melbourne’s inner north, a few hundred nerds dress up in historical armour and attack each other with foam latex swords. It’s live action role play: turbocharged Dungeons & Dragons meets medieval re-enactment.

I’ve been Larping for seven years. It’s the biggest thing in my life outside of comedy, and the two scenes have a lot in common. Everyone’s broke. Everyone was bullied in high school. No one gets into Larp or standup if things are going well.

The biggest commonality is the gatekeeping. A crusted old comic in the corner of a greenroom gasps: “You’re a fan of standup, are you? Name three of Carl Barron’s best jokes.” His Larp counterpart, a polyamorous he/they in a top hat with a cog on it, twirls a cane: “So you like Warhammer Fantasy Battle? Name three spells an Elven cleric can use in combat.” I’d like to see those two sit down and collectively name three women who feel safe around them.

articles.title: Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’
articles.summary: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience. When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries.
body: Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”

There is a term for that post-order clarity: delivery guilt. The pandemic turned food delivery apps such as DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub, once only popular in major cities, into a full-fledged national lifestyle. One Purdue study found that two-thirds of consumers used a food-ordering app at least once in 2024; another recent survey from the marketing company FinanceBuzz in partnership with Bank of America found that 57% of Americans get takeout or delivery weekly or more. Gen Z is more likely to feed the habit, clocking in an average of five orders a month – roughly double the monthly orders made by Boomers.

articles.title: These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine
articles.summary: American resorts are once again having a moment — and it’s not pickleball partisans driving the trend. A new generation of travelers, beset with decision fatigue in their daily lives, are embracing the all-inclusive stay where activities, amenities, and dining are all on the menu and usually just a…
body: Fortunately, stress-free no longer needs to mean bland or generic when it comes to cuisine and culture. Resorts have begun forging deep culinary connections to their surroundings, far beyond merely offering a few regionally specific cocktails or themed burger toppings.

Onsite farms, creameries, and distilleries provide fresh ingredients with true terroir, as well as a new category of resort activity: food-and-drink-focused tours and workshops to fill the time between morning yoga and an afternoon poolside nap.

Some resort restaurants, like Clay at Wildflower Farms in New York’s Hudson Valley and Sierra Mar at the Post Ranch Inn in Big Sur, California, have become destinations in themselves, where star chefs take diners deep into a region’s foodways.
These resorts leave visitors not just relaxed but also satisfied, having truly experienced — and tasted — a particular place.

articles.title: Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts
articles.summary: Plenty of resorts across the country have excellent restaurants, but travelers seeking more should explore the hands-on side of culinary resort experiences. From New York’s Hudson Valley to the South Texas Coast, adventurous food lovers can partake in workshops and experiences that get them out of…
body: Guests today expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

At these properties, it’s less about what’s on your plate and more about how it got there. Big Sur is the perfect place to forage for edible botanicals and aromatics, and on Chesapeake Bay, harvesting and shucking oysters is woven into the community’s cultural fabric. Those wanting to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City can head up to the Hudson Valley for focaccia-making, while a desert oasis on the outskirts of Scottsdale, Arizona, teaches you how to craft pasta like a pro.

No matter your level of expertise, these resort experiences are designed to connect curious travelers with an impressive network of chefs, farmers, ecologists, mixologists, and bakers. For a vacation that will also quench your thirst for knowledge, head to these exciting culinary resorts.

articles.title: The Wildlife Photographer of the Year Is Here, See Microscopic Slime Molds and Giant Elephants
articles.summary: We take a look at the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 winners and highly commended photographs, hand-selected from 65,403 entries ahead of the exhibition
body: Ahead of the 62nd Wildlife Photographer of the Year Exhibition, the Natural History Museum has revealed the winners whose captivating shots will be displayed to the world. The winners have finally been selected from 65,403 entries across 121 countries and territories and will be showcased in an exhibition starting Friday, October 16, 2026.
For the first time in the competition's history, both the adult and young overall winners have been recognized for black-and-white photography.

Italian wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi claims the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 for his powerful image, The Aftermath, featuring a female elephant carrying a deceased calf in Huab River Valley, Namibia. Kathy Moran, chair of the jury, said, “This photograph works on so many levels. Emotionally it’s a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually it’s proof that animals have cognition. This photograph says it all.”

Meanwhile, Oscar Whitfield has been named Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year thanks to Labour of Love, which captures the arduous exertion of a dung beetle pushing its precious cargo using a fast shutter speed and high light sensitivity.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Daisy Edgar-Jones Talks ‘Sense and Sensibility,’ Hair Discourse, and Sisterhood
articles.summary: “Sense and Sensibility” star Daisy Edgar-Jones joined Chloe at the Metrograph in New York on Wednesday for a post-screening live taping of “The Run-Through.”
body: When the Vogue Book Club selected Sense and Sensibility as its latest focus, Chloe’s first question to the staff was: Are you an Elinor or a Marianne? Given Chloe herself identifies as an Elinor—even if she is, by her own admission, Marianne-presenting—it was only fitting that Daisy Edgar-Jones, who plays Elinor in Georgia Oakley’s new adaptation of the classic Jane Austen novel, joined the podcast for a live, post-screening taping at the Metrograph in New York.

Of course, Daisy is no stranger to a book adaptation; her breakout role was in Hulu’s Normal People, based on the novel by Sally Rooney. But Sense and Sensibility marked her first period piece—and her first time being asked to appear barefaced on screen.

“Georgia was like, ‘We’re having no makeup in this film.’ Esmé [Creed-Miles, who plays Marianne] and I were like, ‘Not even ChapStick?’ She was like, ‘Nothing.’ And then Esmé and I would sneak a little bit of ChapStick onto set, and Georgia would be like, ‘Take it off. I can see it!’” Daisy recalled.

articles.title: Nara Smith Regrets Trying to Make Twizzlers
articles.summary: The internet’s queen of from-scratch cooking talks recipe fails, house slippers, and the surprisingly sweet story behind her very specific pancake ritual.
body: In person, she’s far less precious and much funnier. During Smith’s visit to the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen, her relentless pace was on full display. When I ran down a couple of floors to return a pen her producer had left behind, I found her completely transformed, glam fully retouched, already posing for her next shoot for Vanity Fair.

We spoke to Smith about the kitchen slippers hiding beneath her camera frame, the failed homemade Twizzlers that still haunt her, the sudden onset of her egg ick, and the oddly specific way her dad taught her to cut pancakes into tiny squares.

People think I’m wearing heels. I’m actually wearing slippers. I’m very tall, and if I wear heels the counter is too low and nothing looks proportionate. Also, I’m standing all day and my lower back would never forgive me. So it’s always a really good cushioned house slipper. Comfort first.
You spend so much time making food on camera. Are there recipes that feel especially personal to you?
